The Weilüe, a Chinese text composed in the early third century CE, described the Roman Empire (Da Qin) as a distant kingdom located "west of Anxi (Parthia) and Tiaozhi (Characene and Susiana), and west of the Great Sea," accessible by sea from Parthian territory in a journey that could take anywhere from two months to three years depending on wind conditions. [S1] According to this source, the Roman Empire "has more than four hundred smaller cities and towns" and "extends several thousand li in all directions," with its capital located "close to the mouth of a river" and surrounded by "outer walls of the city" made of stone. [S1] A later Chinese historical record, the Hou Hanshu, documented that in 166 CE "the king of Da Qin (the Roman Empire), Andun (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus), sent envoys from beyond the frontiers through Rinan (Commandery on the central Vietnamese coast), to offer elephant tusks, rhinoceros horn, and turtle shell," and noted that "This was the very first time there was [direct] communication [between the two countries]." [S3]

results.answer: In the Weilüe's Classical Chinese, Da Qin is described with several distinctive features. The kingdom "is also called Lijian" and "is west of Anxi (Parthia) and Tiaozhi (Characene and Susiana), and west of the Great Sea" [S1]. The text states that "This country (the Roman Empire) has more than four hundred smaller cities and towns. It extends several thousand li in all directions" [S1]. Regarding its capital, "The king has his capital (that is, the city of Rome) close to the mouth of a river (the Tiber). The outer walls of the city are made of stone" [S1]. The source text itself reads: "大秦國一號犁靬，在安息、條支西大海之西" and describes the kingdom as having "以石爲城郭" [S1].
